the human hand can be accurately modeled and that the soft-tissue artifact can be compensated for.

the proposed kinematic model of a human hand can be calibrated to accurately reconstruct finger postures during grasp and that the hand posture space can be described by a low number of postural synergies.

a) the proposed model is able to reconstruct the human hand kinematics with a good accuracy; b) the proposed soft-tissue compensation mechanism can be calibrated in a systematic manner; and c) the proposed model can be used to study human grasp synergies.

the development of an accurate and reliable methodology to record human finger posturing during grasping, which can be employed for the analysis of hand postural synergy properties, as well as to define effective robotic hand postures or to drive hand avatars in virtual environments.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

this paper presents a methodology for accurate recording of human finger postures, with the potential to be employed in neuroscience studies, in hand animation for avatars, and to provide prior knowledge for robot hand grasps.

a novel methodology has been developed that enables accurate recording of finger postures during grasp, which can be used for the study of hand postural synergy in humans and for the design and control of robotic grasping.
this paper presents a new methodology that allows the accurate recording of human hand postures in grasping, and the systematic analysis of the underlying postural synergies.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a kinematic model reconstructed with magnetic resonance imaging is an excellent tool to record in vivo human finger joint angles with high accuracy, even if markers attached to the fingers are visible.
, in order to accurately measure human hand kinematics, it is essential to account for the soft-tissue artifact, which is a source of significant errors in the estimation of the joint angles.
, in order to obtain reliable data on the human hand kinematics during grasping, a careful calibration is required, which should take into account the effect of soft-tissue artifacts.
